speaker: Tim Latimer
title: Tim Latimer on Solving the Financing Problem for Geothermal
question: In capital-intensive clean energy deployment, how is the private financing market closing the "missing middle" gap between early venture capital and traditional project finance?
guest: If you think back 15 years ago to the Clean Tech 1.0 bust, one of the failure modes was that a bunch of venture capital went into technologies that took a long time to develop, and there wasn't really a pass-the-baton of who the next source of capital was going to be. People talk about the missing middle or the valley of death, but market inefficiencies—if there's money to be made—don't last for long. What we're seeing right now is a bunch of venture capitalists who historically only played in Series A, B, and C recognizing that there's a capital gap for second-of-a-kind and third-of-a-kind deployment, so they've raised continuity or growth funds to piggyback off their successful companies. Meanwhile, traditional infrastructure investors who only wanted to do the tenth project realized that if they wanted to sell their LPs on getting a differentiated return, they needed to step into projects earlier, so they've raised funds to come in one click earlier. That valley of death is closing from both sides—there's still a gap, but it's being converged on from both directions.

points.core: Early clean-tech busts occurred because venture-backed hardware lacked follow-on deployment capital.
points.note: Accept: Clean Tech 1.0 failed when VCs funded long-horizon hardware with no next capital provider to pass the baton to. Do not credit: generic statements that clean tech was unprofitable or too early.

points.core: Venture firms now raise continuity funds to finance second-of-a-kind commercial deployments.
points.note: Accept: Series A-C VCs launching growth or continuity vehicles to carry successful hardware startups one step further into early deployment. Do not credit: vague statements that VCs are investing more money.

points.core: Infrastructure investors launch earlier-stage vehicles to deliver differentiated returns for their LPs.
points.note: Accept: traditional PE or infrastructure funds stepping one click earlier than tenth-of-a-kind projects because mature assets no longer offer differentiated LP returns. Do not credit: saying infrastructure funds are suddenly more risk-tolerant without explaining the LP return incentive.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
The gap sits where a technology is proven at pilot scale but still too risky for banks: first-of-a-kind (FOAK) and early commercial plants need tens to hundreds of millions of dollars, too much for venture funds and too unproven for project lenders. Private markets are closing it in a few ways, though only partially.

Specialised funds now target this stage directly, including growth and infrastructure vehicles from climate-focused investors (Breakthrough Energy's Catalyst, Generate Capital, Galvanize, Spring Lane and similar), often using hybrid structures that mix equity, preferred equity and venture debt. Blended and catalytic capital from philanthropies, corporates and public lenders takes first-loss or subordinated positions, drawing in conventional investors. Risk is also being stripped out contractually: long-term offtake agreements and advance purchase commitments from creditworthy buyers, performance and technology insurance, and engineering wraps make revenue and construction risk bankable. Finally, private credit, tax-credit transfer markets and development-company platforms that bundle projects give lenders diversification and scale.

Capital remains thin relative to need, and FOAK projects still struggle most. This is from my general knowledge, not a fresh search.

models.label: Gemini 4 Carbon
models.answer:
In clean energy deployment, the "missing middle" arises around first-of-a-kind (FOAK) commercial facilities that are too capital-intensive for dilutive venture equity yet carry too much technology risk for traditional banks and infrastructure funds. Private markets are closing this gap by assembling bespoke, hybrid capital stacks tailored to early industrial scale-up. 

Dedicated transition-infrastructure and climate growth funds now underwrite early plants directly, targeting mid-teens, infrastructure-plus returns with structured upside rather than demanding venture-style multiples. Alongside them, private credit funds deploy venture debt, equipment leasing, asset-backed mezzanine facilities, and transferable tax-credit bridge loans to fund capital expenditures without excessive equity dilution. To make these structures viable, deals frequently layer catalytic or first-loss capital from family offices, philanthropies, and corporate strategic investors beneath senior debt to absorb early execution risk. Finally, private financiers pair creative capital with commercial risk-transfer mechanisms—including bankable corporate offtake agreements, advance market commitments, engineering performance wraps, and specialized technology-performance insurance—to manufacture predictable cash flows and graduate proven assets into conventional project finance.

noweb.answer: Private markets are bridging clean energy’s "missing middle"—particularly first-of-a-kind commercial plants too capital-intensive for venture equity yet too unproven for bank project finance—through specialized hybrid capital stacks and risk-transfer structures. A growing class of transitional investors, including climate growth-infrastructure funds, equipment financiers, and asset-backed private credit firms, now underwrites early commercial deployment at risk-adjusted returns situated between venture capital and traditional infrastructure. Instead of funding physical plants with dilutive startup equity, developers increasingly isolate assets in special-purpose vehicles structured around blended finance, using catalytic family-office or philanthropic capital as first-loss tranches to attract senior private debt. Strategic corporate partners simultaneously anchor bankability through project-level joint ventures, advance market commitments, and binding offtake contracts that secure predictable revenues. Meanwhile, specialty insurers provide technology performance warranties and completion wraps that substitute for multiyear operating histories, while private bridge lenders monetize transferable tax credits and equipment collateral upfront, shrinking net equity needs until emerging technologies establish the track record conventional project lenders require.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Private investors are closing the "missing middle" mainly by building hybrid capital that sits between venture equity and conventional project debt. One approach is the infrastructure-as-a-service platform. Generate Capital is the clearest example: it uses permanent, patient capital to own and run early commercial assets, then pays for them through long-term service contracts.

A second approach is new fund types aimed at a technology's first commercial plant. Breakthrough Energy Catalyst, TPG Rise Climate, Brookfield's transition funds and growth arms at firms such as Energy Impact Partners write larger checks for these plants. They often mix philanthropic, corporate and institutional money, so the catalytic tranches take the first losses.

Structured and private credit adds venture debt, mezzanine loans, holdco financing and equipment leasing. These are often backed by warranties from technology suppliers or technical performance insurance, which makes risks bankable earlier.

Demand guarantees matter just as much. Long-term offtake deals from buyers such as Microsoft, Google and the Frontier carbon-removal coalition, plus advance purchase commitments, give lenders predictable revenue to lend against.

Public money still often brings in private capital, through DOE loan guarantees, green banks and transferable tax credits. These tools have shrunk or become less certain since 2025 policy changes, so private structuring now carries more of the load.

models.label: Gemini 4 Neon
models.answer: Private markets are closing the "missing middle" for first-of-a-kind (FOAK) clean energy projects—which are too capital-intensive for venture capital yet too risky for traditional project finance—by assembling blended capital stacks and specialized risk-mitigation tools. Rather than relying on a single asset class, developers now layer patient, first-loss, or catalytic capital from family offices, philanthropies, and corporate balance sheets beneath specialized transition infrastructure equity, private credit, mezzanine debt, and equipment finance. To unlock that commercial debt, private insurers are increasingly underwriting technology performance warranties and project completion insurance, transferring technical risk off lenders' balance sheets. Simultaneously, creditworthy corporate buyers and buyers' clubs are providing revenue certainty through long-term offtake agreements and advance market commitments. Finally, dedicated transition-finance platforms and joint ventures with established industrial strategics and engineering, procurement, and construction (EPC) partners are absorbing development and delivery risk, helping early commercial plants achieve the track record needed to graduate to conventional, lower-cost project finance.

They use growth equity, preferred equity, and structured debt to fund engineering, construction, and early operations while taking on risks that conventional project lenders typically avoid.

Dedicated FOAK and climate-infrastructure equity funds now invest directly at the asset or project-development level, accepting higher construction and scale-up risk than traditional infrastructure investors while targeting lower returns than venture equity. Alongside them, private credit and structured-debt funds are stepping in with flexible mezzanine, equipment, and bridge loans—often paired with warrants or milestone-based tranches—that carry projects through commissioning until they can refinance into low-cost, non-recourse project debt. Simultaneously, investors are assembling blended capital stacks where catalytic or philanthropic first-loss capital absorbs early downside to crowd in institutional senior lenders. Finally, strategic corporates and creditworthy buyers are de-risking revenue through long-term offtake agreements, prepayments, and joint-venture equity, while specialized insurers offer technology performance wraps that make novel hardware bankable much earlier.
